pages.text: `x² + 5x + 6` is one `x²` tile, 5 strips and 6 unit squares. With 2 strips along one side and 3 along the other, that is 2 + 3 = 5 strips, and the 2 by 3 corner takes 2 × 3 = 6 squares exactly. The sides read off as the brackets, so `x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3)`, and finding them is [[factorising]].

pages.name: Which brackets?
pages.task: Here are the tiles of `x² + 6x + 8`. Which brackets close them into a rectangle?
pages.why: The strips split into a pair that adds to 6, and the same pair must multiply to 8 to fill the corner. 2 and 4 do both, so `x² + 6x + 8 = (x + 2)(x + 4)`.

pages.alt: The tiles of x squared plus 5x plus 6: 1 x squared tile, 5 strips, 6 unit squares. Put together as a rectangle x plus 3 wide and x plus 3 tall, 4 tiles are missing and 0 are left over. Knobs at the end of each side change its number of strips. strips: needs 6, you have 5. squares: needs 9, you have 6. x plus 3 x plus 3 equals x squared plus 6x plus 9, which is not the quadratic.

pages.text: Of the pairs that multiply to 6, 1 and 6 add to 7, and only 2 and 3 add to 5. An easy slip is `(x + 3)(x + 3)`, since 3 + 3 also makes 6, by adding instead of multiplying, but its rectangle needs 9 squares and 6 strips. Drag the knob at the end of each side to try other pairs.

pages.name: Bigger numbers
pages.task: Now the tiles of `x² + 9x + 20`. Which brackets close them into a rectangle?
pages.why: Of the pairs that multiply to 20, only 4 and 5 add to 9. So the corner is 4 by 5, and `x² + 9x + 20 = (x + 4)(x + 5)`.

pages.alt: A grid for x squared minus x minus 12, filled in backwards: x squared top left and the number on its own bottom right. x times x is x squared. minus 4 times x is minus 4x, hatched. x times 3 is 3x. minus 4 times 3 is minus 12, hatched. minus 4x and 3x add to minus x. x squared minus x minus 12 equals x minus 4 x plus 3. Try x equals 5. x minus 4 x plus 3 makes 1 times 8 equals 8. x squared minus x minus 12 makes 25 minus 5 minus 12 equals 8.

pages.text: A minus sign has no tile, so lesson 1's grid takes over, filled in backwards: `x²` top left, −12 bottom right, and the other two cells must add to `−x`. The corner is below zero, so one number of the pair is negative, and 4 and 3 multiply to 12 and are 1 apart, so the bigger one, 4, takes the minus to make −1. So −4 and 3 multiply to −12 and add to −1, and `x² − x − 12 = (x − 4)(x + 3)`.

pages.name: Minus in the corner
pages.task: Fill the grid backwards for `x² + 2x − 15`. Which brackets is it?
pages.why: The pair must multiply to −15, so one number is below zero, and add to 2. 5 and −3 do both, so `x² + 2x − 15 = (x + 5)(x − 3)`. At `x = 4` both make 9.

pages.text: Take out any common factor first, or the brackets come out as `(2x + 4)(x + 3)`, which still has a 2 inside. The tiles of `2x² + 10x + 12` split into two equal piles, built one after the other, each `x² + 5x + 6`, so `2x² + 10x + 12 = 2(x + 2)(x + 3)`.

pages.name: No squares
pages.task: `x² + 6x` has no unit squares. Which brackets make it?
pages.why: With no squares, all 6 strips lie along one side, so the rectangle is `x` by `x + 6`. That is the common factor `x` taken out, so `x² + 6x = x(x + 6)`.

pages.alt: The tiles of 2x squared plus 7x plus 3: 2 x squared tiles, 7 strips, 3 unit squares. They close into a rectangle 2x plus 1 wide and x plus 3 tall. The blocks are labelled: 2 x² tiles, 6 strips, 1 strip, 3 squares. 2x squared plus 7x plus 3 equals 2x squared plus 6x plus x plus 3. equals 2x x plus 3 plus 1 x plus 3. equals 2x plus 1 x plus 3.

pages.text: With `2x²`, the 2 `x²` tiles sit side by side, 2 by 1, and the 3 squares sit 1 by 3. The strips fill a 2 by 3 block of 6 under the tiles and a 1 by 1 block of 1 beside them, made from the same four numbers, so 6 × 1 = 2 × 3 and the pair must multiply to 6 as well as add to 7. The two columns are `2x(x + 3)` and `1(x + 3)`, so `2x² + 7x + 3 = (2x + 1)(x + 3)`.

pages.name: A number in front
pages.task: `3x² + 10x + 8` has three `x²` tiles. Which brackets close its tiles into a rectangle?
pages.why: The pair must multiply to 3 × 8 = 24 and add to 10, which is 6 and 4. So 6 strips lie under the three `x²` tiles and 4 beside them, and `3x² + 10x + 8 = (3x + 4)(x + 2)`.

pages.alt: A grid for x squared minus 49, filled in backwards: x squared top left and the number on its own bottom right. x times x is x squared. 7 times x is 7x. x times minus 7 is minus 7x, hatched. 7 times minus 7 is minus 49, hatched. The two x cells are outlined: they cancel out. 7x and minus 7x add to 0. x squared minus 49 equals x plus 7 x minus 7.

pages.text: With no `x` term, the two other cells must add to 0, so the pair is a number and its negative, here multiplying to −49. 49 is 7², so `x² − 49` is one square take away another, and the pair is 7 and −7, whose `7x` and `−7x` cancel: `x² − 49 = (x + 7)(x − 7)`, a [[difference of two squares]]. `x² + 4x + 1` has no whole-number pair, since only 1 × 1 and −1 × −1 make 1 and neither adds to 4, so lessons 4 and 5 find its brackets another way.

pages.name: Mixed: a square
pages.why: The pair must multiply to 9 and add to −6, so both numbers are below zero, −3 and −3. Equal numbers make a square, so `x² − 6x + 9 = (x − 3)²`, a [[perfect square]]. At `x = 1` both make 4.

pages.name: Mixed: a common factor
pages.why: Both terms divide by 2, so `2x² − 8 = 2(x² − 4)`. The pair for `x² − 4` adds to 0 and multiplies to −4, which is 2 and −2. So the answer is `2(x + 2)(x − 2)`, and at `x = 3` both make 10.
